opus-5.5.text:
Well, there are a few reasons, and they're all connected. The first is simply that the internet is running out, at least the high-quality part of it. If you look at math specifically, there's a finite amount of well-written problems with clean, verified solutions out there, and frontier models have more or less already seen all of it. So if you want to keep improving reasoning, you can't just scrape harder. You have to make new data.

The second reason is contamination. When a model does well on a benchmark, we honestly don't always know whether it's reasoning or recalling, because so many of those problems, or close variants of them, are floating around online. With synthetic generation we can create problems that are guaranteed not to be in anybody's pretraining corpus, which gives us a much cleaner signal about what the model can actually do.

The third reason, and maybe the one I find most exciting, is control. When you generate problems yourself, you can dial the difficulty up or down, target specific skills, compose concepts in new ways, and build a curriculum instead of taking whatever distribution the internet happens to give you. Internet data is very uneven. There's lots of easy material and then a long, sparse tail of hard material. Synthetic data lets you fill in the gaps where the model is weakest.

And in math there's a nice bonus: verification is relatively tractable. You can often check the answer programmatically or with a stronger solver, so you can filter out the junk. That makes synthetic data less risky in math than in more open-ended domains.

I'll add a caveat, though. Synthetic data isn't magic. If you're careless, you just amplify the model's own biases and blind spots, which is a kind of model collapse. So the real research question isn't whether to use synthetic data. It's how to generate data that is diverse, correct, and actually pushes the model beyond what it already knows. That's where a lot of our effort goes.

r001.rationale: The response says synthetic math data can be checked programmatically or with a stronger solver and that junk can be filtered out, but it does not clearly state that automatically generated solutions may have unknown correctness.

r002.rationale: It says synthetic generation can target specific skills, combine concepts in new ways, build a curriculum, and fill gaps in the internet’s uneven distribution, communicating broader exploration of mathematical reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, there are a couple of reasons. The first is contamination. If you scrape math problems off the internet, there's a very good chance that the model you're evaluating, or the model you're training, has already seen those exact problems, or very close paraphrases of them, somewhere in its pretraining data. So you can't really tell whether the model is reasoning or whether it's just recalling. By generating problems synthetically, we know they're fresh, and we can actually measure generalization.

The second reason is control. When you rely on what happens to exist online, you get whatever distribution the internet gives you, and that distribution is pretty skewed. There are a lot of problems of a certain style, a certain difficulty, a lot of GSM8K-flavored word problems, and not much systematic coverage. With synthetic generation we can dial the difficulty, we can compose problems out of specific sub-skills, we can vary surface form while holding the underlying structure fixed, and we can go to scale. If we want a million problems that all require, say, a particular combination of algebraic manipulation and multi-step planning, we can just make them.

And there's a third thing, which is a little more philosophical. Human-written problems are written for humans. They test the things that are hard for people. But the failure modes of language models are often different from ours. Models can be very good at things humans find hard and very brittle on things humans find trivial. So if you want to probe where models actually break, you often have to construct the problems yourself, because nobody on the internet bothered to write down problems that no human would find interesting but that happen to expose a real gap in the model.

Now, the obvious worry is quality. Synthetic data can be wrong, or it can be repetitive and bland, and if you're not careful you end up training a model on its own mistakes. So we spend a lot of effort on verification, on making sure the answers are actually correct, and on diversity, so the generator isn't just producing the same template over and over with different numbers. But if you get those pieces right, I think synthetic generation gives you something you simply cannot get from scraping, which is a controlled, uncontaminated, and essentially unlimited source of problems.

r001.rationale: The response says synthetic data can be wrong and emphasizes verifying answers, but it does not state that automatically generated solutions to difficult math problems may have unknown correctness.

r002.rationale: It explains that internet problems have skewed, limited coverage, while synthetic generation can compose problems from specific sub-skills and vary difficulty and structure to explore more reasoning.

astra-6.text:
The internet has a lot of math problems, but it gives you limited control over their difficulty and diversity. You can end up with many variations of the same kind of problem, and you may not know whether a model has already seen them during training.

Generating problems synthetically lets us vary the underlying structure, control the complexity, and, when we have a reliable procedure for constructing them, verify the answers. That helps us ask a more precise question: Is the model learning how to solve this class of problems, and can it generalize to new combinations or harder instances?

r001.rationale: The response says synthetic answers can be verified with a reliable construction procedure, but does not state that automatically generated solutions to difficult problems may have unknown correctness.

r002.rationale: It explains that synthetic generation varies problem structure and supports testing new combinations and harder instances, conveying a broader and more diverse range of mathematical reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
The main reason is that we want to control what the model has seen and what it hasn’t. With problems from the internet, it’s hard to know whether a model has encountered the same problem, or a very similar one, during training. So if it gets the answer right, is it reasoning, or is it recalling something?

By generating problems synthetically, we can systematically vary their structure and difficulty, and test whether the model can generalize to new combinations. We can also generate the correct answers, which makes it easier to evaluate at scale.

r001.rationale: The response says synthetic generation lets them generate correct answers; it does not say automatically generated solutions may have unknown correctness.

r002.rationale: It says synthetic generation lets them vary problem structure and difficulty and test generalization to new combinations, conveying exploration across a broader range of mathematical reasoning.
